articles.surfaceLabel: Does South Africa's Privacy Law Apply to Your Organization?
articles.plainSummary: POPIA applies to almost anyone processing personal information in South Africa, in the public or private sector. Uniquely, it also protects companies and other legal entities, not just people.
articles.professionalLayer: POPIA applies to responsible parties domiciled in South Africa, and to those abroad that use automated or non-automated means located in South Africa beyond mere forwarding. It is built on eight conditions for lawful processing: accountability, processing limitation, purpose specification, further processing limitation, information quality, openness, security safeguards, and data subject participation. Distinctively, personal information includes information about existing juristic persons, extending protection to companies. Every organization must register an information officer with the Information Regulator, and certain high-risk processing requires prior authorization. Penalties reach R10 million or imprisonment for serious offences.
articles.assessTrigger: Have you registered an information officer with the Regulator, checked whether any processing needs prior authorization, and accounted for juristic-person data in scope?

gapRemediation.smb: Register your information officer, usually the head of the business by default, and work through the eight conditions as a checklist.
gapRemediation.midMarket: Screen processing against the prior-authorization triggers, which include some credit reporting and criminal-data processing.
gapRemediation.enterprise: Maintain a POPIA condition-mapped control framework and include juristic-person data, which global programs usually exclude.

comparisonFlags.note: POPIA protects juristic persons such as companies, not only natural persons.

articles.surfaceLabel: Why Organizations Are Allowed to Use Your Information in South Africa
articles.plainSummary: POPIA allows processing on grounds familiar from GDPR: your consent, a contract, a legal duty, protecting your legitimate interests, public tasks, or the organization's legitimate interests.
articles.professionalLayer: Section 11 permits processing where the data subject consents, processing is necessary for a contract with the data subject, complies with a legal obligation, protects a legitimate interest of the data subject, is necessary for a public law duty, or is necessary to pursue legitimate interests of the responsible party or a third party. Consent means voluntary, specific, informed expression of will, and the data subject may object on reasonable grounds to legitimate-interest and public-duty processing. Special personal information, including religion, race, health, biometrics, and criminal behavior, is prohibited unless a specific authorization applies, and children's information carries its own regime.
articles.assessTrigger: Is each processing activity mapped to a Section 11 ground, with special-information authorizations and objection handling documented?

gapRemediation.smb: Map activities to the six grounds, mirroring GDPR work you may have done, and check special-information rules.
gapRemediation.midMarket: Stand up objection handling for legitimate-interest processing, which South African practice actively uses.
gapRemediation.enterprise: Integrate POPIA grounds into your global basis register with the special-information authorization layer.

articles.surfaceLabel: Your Right to See Your Information in South Africa
articles.plainSummary: You can ask an organization to confirm, free of charge, whether it holds your personal information, and to give you the record itself within a reasonable time.
articles.professionalLayer: Section 23 entitles a data subject, on proof of identity, to obtain free confirmation of whether a responsible party holds their personal information, and to receive the record or a description of it within a reasonable time, at a prescribed fee if any, in a reasonable format, and with advice of the right to request correction. Access requests operate alongside the Promotion of Access to Information Act, and the request forms and fee structures come from that interplay. Refusal grounds track PAIA's protections such as privilege and third-party privacy.
articles.responseTimeline: Within a reasonable time. PAIA procedures apply a 30-day framework to formal requests.
articles.assessTrigger: Can you confirm holdings free of charge and produce records within the PAIA-aligned timeframe, using the prescribed request forms?

gapRemediation.smb: Publish a simple access route and use the standard forms. Free confirmation is the piece most often missed.
gapRemediation.midMarket: Align POPIA access with your PAIA manual and fee schedule, which the Regulator expects to exist.
gapRemediation.enterprise: Route South African requests through DSR tooling with PAIA-compliant forms, fees, and refusal grounds.

articles.surfaceLabel: Your Right to Correct or Delete Your Information in South Africa
articles.plainSummary: You can ask for your information to be corrected or for information that is inaccurate, excessive, out of date, or unlawfully held to be deleted or destroyed.
articles.professionalLayer: Section 24 allows a data subject to request correction of personal information, and deletion or destruction of information that is inaccurate, irrelevant, excessive, out of date, incomplete, misleading, obtained unlawfully, or that the responsible party is no longer authorized to retain. The responsible party must comply as soon as reasonably practicable, or provide credible evidence supporting the information, and where a dispute remains unresolved, attach an indication that correction was requested but not made. Recipients of the information must be informed of changes where reasonably practicable.
articles.responseTimeline: As soon as reasonably practicable after the request.
articles.assessTrigger: Can you correct or destroy records on the Section 24 grounds, annotate unresolved disputes, and notify past recipients?

gapRemediation.smb: Act on correction requests promptly and keep a note where you decline with your supporting evidence.
gapRemediation.midMarket: Add dispute annotation and recipient notification to your correction workflow.
gapRemediation.enterprise: Automate correction propagation with dispute flags and recipient notices across systems.

articles.surfaceLabel: What Happens When Your Data Is Compromised in South Africa
articles.plainSummary: When there are reasonable grounds to believe your personal information has been accessed or acquired by an unauthorized person, the organization must notify the Regulator and you as soon as reasonably possible.
articles.professionalLayer: Section 22 requires notification of security compromises to the Information Regulator and affected data subjects as soon as reasonably possible after discovery, where there are reasonable grounds to believe personal information has been accessed or acquired by an unauthorized person. Individual notification may be delayed only where a public body responsible for law enforcement or the Regulator determines it would impede a criminal investigation. Notices must provide sufficient information to allow protective measures, including the possible consequences and the identity of the unauthorized person if known. The Regulator provides an eServices portal for compromise notifications.
articles.responseTimeline: Regulator and individuals: as soon as reasonably possible after discovery.
articles.assessTrigger: Does your incident plan cover the Section 22 dual notification with the prescribed content, including identity of the intruder where known?

gapRemediation.smb: Add the Regulator's portal to your breach checklist and use the Section 22 content items as your notice template.
gapRemediation.midMarket: Define the reasonable-grounds trigger in your triage so notification is not delayed by over-investigation.
gapRemediation.enterprise: Encode POPIA's threshold and content requirements in the incident workflow beside fixed-clock regimes.

articles.surfaceLabel: Moving Personal Data Out of South Africa
articles.plainSummary: Personal information may leave South Africa only if the recipient is bound by similar protections, you consent, the transfer is needed for a contract, or it benefits you and consent is impracticable.
articles.professionalLayer: Section 72 prohibits transfer of personal information to a third party in a foreign country unless one of five conditions holds: the recipient is subject to law, binding corporate rules, or a binding agreement providing substantially similar protection including onward-transfer limits; the data subject consents; the transfer is necessary for the performance of a contract with the data subject; it is necessary for a contract in the data subject's interest between the responsible party and a third party; or it is for the data subject's benefit where consent is not reasonably practicable and would likely be given. The substantially-similar-protection test makes vendor contract review the operational core of South African transfer compliance.
articles.assessTrigger: Does each cross-border flow rest on a documented Section 72 condition, with recipient agreements meeting the substantially-similar test including onward transfers?

gapRemediation.smb: Add POPIA-aligned protection clauses to foreign vendor contracts or rely on consent captured at collection.
gapRemediation.midMarket: Inventory outbound flows and record the Section 72 condition each relies on.
gapRemediation.enterprise: Standardize binding agreement language meeting the substantially-similar test across the vendor estate.
